You are a subagent spawned by another session.
Implement Phase E2 (Console Base) of the Financial Resilience Engine in "/Users/ajeet/Projects/Hackathons/Sheridan Datathon 2026". This is a React 19 / Vite 6 / TypeScript 5.7 strict / Tailwind 3.4 / Vitest app. Phase E1 is complete: public/data/engine/profiles.json (4,500 profiles, ~4.7 MB) with contract docs/profiles-schema.md. Read docs/architecture.md, docs/profiles-schema.md, docs/tangerine-challenge.md, docs/decisions.md first, plus existing src/ patterns (src/data/loaders.ts, checksum.ts, src/App.tsx, src/index.css, tailwind.config.js).

## Design guidance (frontend-design skill)
- Ground everything in the subject: this is a weather forecasting system for personal finance. The console is an instrument panel, not a generic dashboard. Distinctive, opinionated choices are welcome, but there is an existing visual system (rp- tokens in src/index.css, Tailwind config): extend it with a cp- token block for console surfaces rather than inventing a second palette.
- Typography and structure should encode meaning: verdict bands are the hero signal (icon + color readable from 2 m away across a judging table). The signature element for E2 is the verdict badge + shocked runway number that visibly changes when a preset is played.
- Copy: plain verbs, sentence case, user-side framing. Every shocked runway number is labeled "steady state". Error and empty states explain what to do (e.g. "Type an account id, for example 68257").
- Quality floor: responsive, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, no inline money math in components (pure functions in src/lib only).

## Content rule (hard): NO em dashes, en dashes, minus sign equivalents, double hyphens, or spaced hyphens in ANY string you write (UI copy, comments, docs). Numeric minus in formatted money is allowed.

## User-confirmed decisions
1. Verdict bands (contiguous, integer deci-month thresholds): critical = buffer_depleted or <10; storm_warning = 10 to 29; watch = 30 to 59; fair_skies = 60 to 119; clear = no_shortfall or >=120 (12.0+ months).
2. One-off semantics per challenge doc EXACTLY: one-off costs subtract from buffer only (buffer_left = B - one_off), never from monthly spending; billsDeltaPct adds scaleCents(H, pct) to spending_after; extraMonthlyCost is recurring spending; income_after = jobLoss ? scaleCents(I, eiPct, 100) : I.

## Architecture to implement (from tech-lead design)

Components/files:
| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| src/data/profiles.ts | Types (AccountProfile per schema doc, ProfilesArtifact with derived ids[] and byId Map), parseProfilesArtifact (strict, named errors per schema checklist), loadProfiles, loadSharedProfiles (module memo, clears on failure), searchAccountIds |
| src/data/profiles.test.ts | Refusal cases (wrong schema_version, extra keys, fractional cents, bad enum, count mismatch), real artifact parse, PLUS baseline cross-check: for all 4,500 profiles runway(buffer_cents, 0, income_cents, spending_cents) equals artifact runway_state/runway_deci_months |
| src/lib/shocks.ts | roundHalfUp (mirror of Python metrics.round_half_up: sign split, ties away from zero), scaleCents, runway() exact twin of scripts/engine/shocks.py: buffer_left<=0 -> buffer_depleted/0; gap<=0 -> no_shortfall/1200; else min((20*buffer_left + gap) // (2*gap), 1200); Twist interface {jobLoss, incomeFactor (0-1 step 0.05, default 0.55), billsDeltaPct (0-100), oneOffMonthsTenths (0-30, 10=1 month of S), extraMonthlyCents, durationMonths (display only)}; IDLE_TWIST; normalizeTwist (quantize incomeFactor to hundredths, eiPct = Math.round(incomeFactor*100) at math boundary, clamp all); applyTwist(profile, twist) -> ShockResult {incomeAfterCents, spendingAfterCents, oneOffCents, bufferLeftCents, gapAfterCents, runway} |
| src/lib/shocks.test.ts | Unit cases: ties, zero income, negative buffer, cap, branch precedence (buffer_depleted wins over no_shortfall) |
| src/lib/shocks.golden.test.ts | Cross-language contract reading scripts/engine/golden_fixtures.json: (1) runway(expected.buffer_cents, 0, expected.income_cents, expected.spending_cents) deep equals expected runway_state/deci_months for all 5 fixtures; (2) medianCents/meanCents twins over the fixture's recorded sorted cents arrays equal expected metric fields (pin the half-cent tie account 23838); (3) branch cases incl. cap (fixture 49900) and deci half tie buffer_left 3 gap 20 -> deci 2; (4) worked example: fixture 68257 combo preset (income_after 357679, bills_delta 64601, spending_after 780685, gap_after 423006, deci 15) and layoff+repair 1.0 month (buffer_left -72299, buffer_depleted, deci 0) |
| src/lib/shockPresets.ts | PresetId = 'layoff' | 'cost_spike' | 'emergency_repair' | 'combo'; SHOCK_PRESETS with label, card (judge-readable twist card sentence), twist: layoff {jobLoss, incomeFactor 0.55, duration 6}; cost_spike {billsDeltaPct 15}; emergency_repair {oneOffMonthsTenths 10}; combo {jobLoss, incomeFactor 0.55, billsDeltaPct 15, duration 6} |
| src/lib/verdict.ts | VerdictBandId/VerdictBand {id, label, glyph, tailwind, threshold}, VERDICT_BANDS, verdictBand(runway) with the confirmed boundaries |
| src/lib/verdict.test.ts | Boundaries at deci 10/30/60/120 and both special states |
| src/lib/planText.ts | buildPlanText(profile, result, twist, band) -> {goal: string[], backup: string[]}. Simple honest templates: goal block = 3 x S starter cushion in dollars + monthly surplus/deficit statement; backup block = baseline vs shocked runway, shocked monthly gap, and when durationMonths > 0 whether runway covers the horizon. No lever machinery (that is E4). |
| src/lib/planText.test.ts | Exact string assertions + dash rule |
| src/lib/format.ts (modify) | formatDeciMonths(deci, state): finite "9.8 months", no_shortfall "120+ months", buffer_depleted "0.0 months"; formatCents handles negatives |
| src/state/consoleStore.ts | Zustand 5 store: status/error/bundle/query/selectedId/twist/activePresetId; actions boot() (idempotent), setQuery, selectAccount (validate against byId), applyPreset, setTwistField (normalize + recompute activePresetId = preset whose twist deep equals current, else null), resetTwist (keeps account), resetAll. Derived values NOT stored; ConsoleView uses useMemo. Comment block reserving E6 keys: R reset twist, Shift+R reset all, 1-4 presets, slash focus lookup, Esc clear, N random account. NO listeners in E2. DOM hooks: id="account-lookup" on search input, data-preset attributes, type="button" everywhere. |
| src/state/consoleStore.test.ts | Transitions with stubbed loader; preset deviation clears activePresetId; reset semantics |
| src/components/console/ConsoleView.tsx | Shell: boot flow (loading/error/ready), layout, pure derivation wiring via useMemo |
| src/components/console/AccountLookup.tsx | Search input + suggestion list (prefix/substring filter over 4,500 ids, no fuzzy lib) |
| src/components/console/BaselineCard.tsx | Current conditions: I, F, S, B, H, P, gap, runway + verdict band, five flag chips, history span, recorded provenance line (check_sum labeled "recorded", never "verified": the browser cannot recompute it) |
| src/components/console/ShockPanel.tsx | 4 preset buttons (cards showing the twist card sentence), sliders (income %, bills %, one-off months of S, extra monthly cost), before/after numbers (income_after, spending_after, one_off, buffer_left, gap_after), shocked runway + band, reset button. Runway labeled "steady state". |
| src/components/console/VerdictBadge.tsx | Band label + glyph + runway label, shared |
| src/components/console/PlanCard.tsx | Goal and backup blocks |
| src/components/console/console.smoke.test.ts | jsdom boot with stubbed fetch: lookup selects account, preset applies, verdict changes, plan renders |
| src/App.tsx (modify) | Mount ConsoleView as the ONLY surface; header reads "Resilience Weather Station" (or similar weather station title); footer cites profiles.json pipeline. Old FindingsView/PlayView stay in tree but unmounted. |
| src/app.smoke.test.ts (modify) | Rewrite for console shell (existing stub-fetch pattern; regex already matches profiles.json) |
| src/index.css (modify) | cp- token block reusing the existing rp- palette (cards, slider, band colors) |
| package.json | npm install zustand (confirm typecheck green first as baseline) |

Data flow: one fetch of dataBase() + "data/engine/profiles.json" -> parseProfilesArtifact -> byId Map -> store boot -> lookup -> pure derivation (useMemo: applyTwist -> verdictBand -> buildPlanText) -> presentational views (zero math in JSX).

Also add a dash scan test over new source files (code points for em dash/en dash/double hyphen/spaced hyphen; allow numeric minus in formatted money).

## Verification (run all, report results)
1. `npx vitest run` (all tests incl. golden fixture cross-language + 4,500 profile cross-check)
2. `npm run typecheck` (or npx tsc --noEmit if no script)
3. `npm run build` (or npx vite build)
4. `uv run pytest -q` and `uv run python -m scripts.engine.verify` (must stay green; no Python changes)
5. Confirm profiles.json fetches under the Pages base path pattern used by existing loaders.

Do NOT modify anything under scripts/engine/ or public/data/engine/.

If you need clarification or encounter ambiguity, output your questions in this exact format at the TOP of your response:

## QUESTIONS FOR USER
- Q1: [your question]

Then continue with your best-effort output based on available information.

Report: files created/modified, test results (counts), build result, typecheck result, key UI decisions (how the verdict band reads from 2m, layout), and any deviations from the design with rationale.

<skill_content name="frontend-design">
# Skill: frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.

## Ground it in the subject

If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.

Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again

For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.

2: 
3: Field by field contract for the Phase E2 loader. The artifact lives at
4: `public/data/engine/profiles.json`, is written by
5: `uv run python -m scripts.engine.build`, and is gated by
6: `uv run python -m scripts.engine.verify`.
7: 
8: ## Guarantees
9: 
10: - Compact JSON (no spaces), one trailing newline, LF line endings.
11: - No timestamps and no floating point values anywhere: two consecutive
12:   builds of unchanged sources are byte identical.
13: - `profiles` keys are account id strings in ascending numeric order.
14: - Every money value is an integer in CAD cents. Every runway value is an
15:   integer count of tenths of a month.
16: - Sources are verified against `data/tangerine/SHA256SUMS` before any row
17:   is read; a mismatch fails the build loudly.
18: 
19: ## Top level shape
20: 
21: ```json
22: {
23:   "meta": {
24:     "schema_version": 1,
25:     "generated_by": "scripts.engine.build",
26:     "sources": [
27:       {"path": "data/tangerine/monthly_summary.csv", "sha256": "64 hex chars", "rows": 185326},
28:       {"path": "data/tangerine/loans.csv", "sha256": "64 hex chars", "rows": 682},
29:       {"path": "data/tangerine/accounts.csv", "sha256": "64 hex chars", "rows": 4500}
30:     ],
31:     "account_count": 4500,
32:     "date_range": {"start": "2020-01", "end": "2025-12"},
33:     "money_unit": "integer CAD cents",
34:     "runway_unit": "tenths of a month",
35:     "rounding": "...",
36:     "definitions": {"income_cents": "...", "runway_deci_months": "..."},
37:     "checksum_recipe": "...",
38:     "edge_flag_counts": {"pensioner": 740, "thin_history": 377, "zero_income": 14,
39:                          "defaulted_loan": 45, "negative_buffer": 23}
40:   },
41:   "profiles": {
42:     "20111": {"account_id": "20111", "income_cents": 0}
43:   }
44: }
45: ```
46: 
47: ## meta block
48: 
49: - `schema_version` (int): currently `1`. The E2 loader must refuse any
50:   other value instead of guessing.
51: - `generated_by` (string): always `scripts.engine.build`.
52: - `sources` (array of 3): one entry per canonical CSV in fixed order
53:   (monthly_summary, loans, accounts) with `path`, `sha256` (64 lowercase
54:   hex), `rows` (data rows, header excluded).
55: - `account_count` (int): equals the number of entries in `profiles`.
56: - `date_range` (object): `start` and `end` as `YYYY-MM`, the minimum
57:   `history.first_month` and maximum `history.last_month` over all
58:   profiles.
59: - `money_unit` (string): `integer CAD cents`.
60: - `runway_unit` (string): `tenths of a month`, so 1200 means 120.0
61:   months.
62: - `rounding` (string): the human readable rounding contract. Dollars
63:   convert to cents with `np.rint(dollars * 100)` (half to even), and
64:   every median, mean, and runway division afterwards uses
65:   ROUND_HALF_UP (ties away from zero) exactly once at the metric
66:   boundary.
67: - `definitions` (object): judge definitions for `income_cents`,
68:   `fixed_costs_cents`, `spending_cents`, `buffer_cents`,
69:   `household_bills_cents`, `loan_payment_cents`, `gap_cents`,
70:   `runway_deci_months`. These strings are duplicated on purpose in
71:   `scripts/engine/verify.py`; drift fails verification.
72: - `checksum_recipe` (string): the provenance recipe (see below).
73: - `edge_flag_counts` (object): accounts per flag across the whole
74:   dataset. The E2 UI should treat a count of 0 as "this flag never fires
75:   in this data". All five are nonzero in the shipped build.

78: 
79: Exactly these keys, no more, no less:

81: ### Identity and judge metrics
82: 
83: - `account_id` (string): digits, matches the key.
84: - `income_cents` (int): I, median of `money_in` over all monthly rows.
85: - `fixed_costs_cents` (int): F, median over months of the per row sum
86:   `household_bills + insurance + loan_payments`. Part 1 display only,
87:   never used in the runway.
88: - `spending_cents` (int): S, median of `money_out` over all rows.
89: - `buffer_cents` (int): B, mean of `avg_daily_balance` over the last
90:   `min(6, n)` rows sorted by month, rounded half up. May be negative.
91: - `household_bills_cents` (int): H, median of `household_bills`.
92: - `loan_payment_cents` (int): P, `monthly_payment` when the loan status
93:   is `C` or `D` (running at the end of 2025), otherwise 0. Accounts with
94:   no loan are 0.
95: - `insurance_cents` (int): median of `insurance`.
96: - `loan_payments_median_cents` (int): median of `loan_payments`.
97: - `pension_in_cents` (int): sum of `pension_in` over all rows, not a
98:   median and not windowed.
99: - `gap_cents` (int): S minus I. Positive means typical spending exceeds
100:   typical income.
101: 
102: ### Runway (baseline, before any shock)
103: 
104: - `runway_state` (string): exactly one of `finite`, `no_shortfall`,
105:   `buffer_depleted`.
106: - `runway_deci_months` (int): 0 for `buffer_depleted`, 1200 for
107:   `no_shortfall`, otherwise `ROUND_HALF_UP(10 * buffer_left / gap)`
108:   capped at 1200. Branch order is fixed: `buffer_left <= 0` first, then
109:   `gap <= 0`, then the finite branch. The E3 shock engine must reuse
110:   this branch order so live shock numbers match the artifact baseline.
111: 
112: ### history
113: 
114: - `history.first_month`, `history.last_month` (string): `YYYY-MM`.
115: - `history.row_count` (int): monthly rows, at least 1, at most 72.
116: - `history.months_contiguous` (bool): true when the sorted months fill
117:   one unbroken span (true for every account in the shipped build).
118: - `history.months` (array of `YYYY-MM`, optional): present only when
119:   `months_contiguous` is false, one entry per row in month order.
120: 
121: ### loan
122: 
123: `null` when the account has no row in `loans.csv`, otherwise an object:
124: 
125: - `loan_id` (int), `status` (string `A`, `B`, `C`, `D`),
126:   `defaulted` (bool, true for `B` and `D`),
127:   `amount_cents` (int), `duration_months` (int),
128:   `monthly_payment_cents` (int), `loan_start` (string `YYYY-MM-DD`),
129:   `scheduled_end_month` (string `YYYY-MM`, `loan_start` month plus
130:   `duration_months`).

132: The P rule reads `status` only: `C` or `D` pays, `A` or `B` is 0. The
133: build report logs the schedule versus status disagreement count so a
134: future data refresh that breaks the rule shows up immediately (0
135: disagreements in the shipped build).
136:

138: 
139: Exactly five booleans:
140: 
141: - `pensioner`: `pension_in_cents > 0`.
142: - `thin_history`: `row_count < 18`, a quarter of the 72 month dataset
143:   span. The B window itself is still `min(6, n)` rows regardless of this
144:   flag.
145: - `zero_income`: `income_cents == 0`.
146: - `defaulted_loan`: `loan.status == "D"` (no loan means false).
147: - `negative_buffer`: `buffer_cents < 0`.
148: 
149: ### balance_series
150: 
151: - `start_month` (string): month of the first value.
152: - `values_cents` (array of int): the last `min(12, row_count)`
153:   `avg_daily_balance` values in month order. Chart input for the E2
154:   profile view.
155: 
156: ### provenance
157: 
158: - `source` (string): `data/tangerine/monthly_summary.csv`.
159: - `filter` (string): `account_id = <id> ordered by month ascending`.
160: - `agg` (string): judge aggregation text, ends with
161:   `checksum value = money_in_cents`.
162: - `check_sum` (string): 64 lowercase hex.
163: 
164: Recompute recipe (mirrored by `src/data/checksum.ts`): build row ids
165: `<account_id>:<month>`, sort them ascending, pair each with the row's

167: UTF-8 bytes.

171: 1. `JSON.parse` the fetch of `profiles.json` (single bundled file, no

# Skill: frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.

## Ground it in the subject

If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.

Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again

For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.

41: - **Deterministic offline artifact.** profiles.json carries no
42:   timestamps, no randomness, and no floats; two consecutive builds are
43:   byte identical. All data is bundled for an offline booth.
44: - **Checksummed sources fail loud.** The three canonical CSVs are
45:   verified against data/tangerine/SHA256SUMS before any row is read.
46: - **Any account must work.** All 4500 accounts, including the five edge
47:   flags (pensioner, thin history, zero income, defaulted loan, negative
48:   buffer), must render without a special case.
49: - **Content convention:** no em dashes, en dashes, minus signs, double
50:   hyphens, or spaced hyphens in shipped strings. verify.py scans the
51:   artifact and exits non zero on a violation.
52: - **Static hosting only.** GitHub Pages, no server, no runtime network
53:   calls beyond bundled assets.
54: 
55: ## Stack
56: 
57: - Python 3.14 + uv + pandas + numpy for the offline engine pipeline;
58:   pytest for tests. Modules are header-style, snake_case, type hinted.
59: - React 19, Vite 6, TypeScript 5.7 strict, Tailwind 3.4, Zustand 5,
60:   Vitest for the site.
61: - three 0.170 + @react-three/fiber is legacy from the dropped game
62:   layer (PlayView); not part of the engine surface.
63: - GitHub Pages via GitHub Actions, base path aware.
64: - Entire for graph queries, checkpoints, and the build trail.
65: 
66: ## Phases E1 to E7
67: 
68: - **E1 profile precompute (COMPLETE).** scripts/engine loads checksum
69:   verified CSVs, computes the judge metrics in integer cents, and
70:   writes public/data/engine/profiles.json (meta plus one profile per
71:   account). Shipped and verified Nov 07 2026.
72: - **E2 console base.** Account lookup over 4500 ids, baseline card,
73:   shock presets plus sliders, verdict, and plan text.
74: - **E3 weather viz.** Forecast strip, storm front, landfall pin,
75:   verdict bands, and the EI-cliff overlay.
76: - **E4 plan engine.** Goal math plus backup levers with +N months
77:   effects.
78: - **E5 Storm Atlas.** Population headline plus strip-plot drill-down.
79: - **E6 judge mode.** Keyboard shortcuts, edge-account guards,
80:   rehearsal, and paper fallback.
81: - **E7 Solana A+ touch.** Gated memo package plus honest receipt badge
82:   in the verdict card.
83: 
84: ### Considered enhancements (secondary)
85: 
86: - **Natural language shock input via the Gemini API.** User provided
87:   idea, secondary to the approved phase list above, and not yet
88:   scheduled. A judge or user types a phrase like "laid off and rent up
89:   15%" and it maps to the twist fields incomeFactor, billsDeltaPct,
90:   and oneOffMonthsOfSpend instead of clicking preset buttons. Risks:
91:   live API dependency at the booth (network is allowed but must never
92:   be required, so it must degrade gracefully to the preset buttons);
93:   parsing must be validated against the twist schema before applying;
94:   and it belongs after E2 where the shock presets exist.
95: 
96: ## Data layer
97: 
98: ```
99: data/tangerine/*.csv (checksums in SHA256SUMS)
100:     -> scripts/engine/load.py      (verify, integer cent parse, grouping)
101:     -> scripts/engine/metrics.py   (pure I, F, S, B, H, gap, flags)
102:     -> scripts/engine/shocks.py    (pure runway function)
103:     -> scripts/engine/build.py     (meta + profiles, deterministic)
104:     -> public/data/engine/profiles.json
105:     -> scripts/engine/verify.py    (naive csv recompute, drift diff, SHA256)
106: ```
107: 
108: - Sources: monthly_summary.csv (185,326 rows), loans.csv (682),
109:   accounts.csv (4,500), over 2020-01 to 2025-12.
110: - The artifact: about 4.7 MB compact JSON, 4500 profiles, meta block
111:   with sources, definitions, checksum recipe, and edge flag counts
112:   (pensioner 740, thin_history 377, zero_income 14, defaulted_loan 45,
113:   negative_buffer 23 in the shipped build).
114: - Loan cross check in the build report: 448 loans running by the status
115:   rule (C or D), 448 running by schedule (end month past 2025-12), 0
116:   disagreements.
117: - Provenance: each profile carries a check_sum over
118:   `account_id:month` rows and `money_in` cents, recipe in
119:   pipeline_lib.checksum and mirrored by src/data/checksum.ts.
120: - Existing site data (world.json, transactions.json, findings.json,
121:   model_card.json) is unchanged; the engine adds public/data/engine/.
122: 
123: ## Verification
124: 
125: - `uv run python -m scripts.engine.build`: checksum gate, build report
126:   with source sha256 prefixes, edge flag counts (all five must be
127:   nonzero), loan cross check, artifact size, PASS line.
128: - `uv run python -m scripts.engine.verify`: independent naive csv
129:   recomputation of all 4500 accounts with no pandas, no numpy, and no
130:   import of scripts.engine.metrics; exact field by field diff; dash
131:   violation scan over every artifact string; prints the artifact SHA256;
132:   exits non zero on any drift.
133: - `uv run pytest -q`: golden fixtures asserted against both
134:   metrics.pipeline and the shipped artifact entry (five real accounts
135:   covering odd and even medians, the half cent tie, thin history with
136:   zero income, a running loan, a defaulted loan, and every runway
137:   branch), schema validation, check_sum recomputation for all accounts,
138:   determinism (two consecutive builds byte identical and equal to the
139:   shipped file).
140: - `scripts/engine/test_metrics.py`: rounding ties, every runway branch
141:   including buffer_depleted, no_shortfall, cap and deci half ties, thin
142:   history buffer, flag thresholds.
143: - Rule drift guard: contract strings in verify.py are duplicated from
144:   build.py on purpose, so a silent edit to a definition fails
145:   verification.
146: 
147: ## Frontend layering
148: 
149: 1. **Data (src/data):** typed loaders with schema validation
150:    (profiles loader lands in E2), checksum mirror, resolveRows for
151:    provenance. No math, no React.
152: 2. **Core (src/lib):** pure functions only. The E2 shock math and E4
153:    plan math live here as TypeScript twins of the Python rules; they
154:    must never import React and must operate on integer cents.
155: 3. **Views (src/components):** engine console view (E2), weather
156:    forecast views (E3), Storm Atlas (E5). Views render numbers from
157:    loaders and core functions; inline money math in a component is a
158:    review failure. Old report and game views are dropped as surfaces.
159: 4. **Render (src/components/river, scene):** presentation only, swappable
160:    without touching layers 1 to 3.
161: 
162: Load once, memoize: profiles.json is fetched a single time and parsed
163: once per session (the same pattern as loadSharedFindingsReport).
164: 
165: ## Performance budget
166: 
167: - Artifact: keep profiles.json under 5 MB and a single request; parse
168:   once, index 4500 account ids for search under 10 ms.
169: - Shock recalculation: integer arithmetic, under 1 ms per interaction,
170:   no async hop for a slider move.
171: - Existing game budget unchanged: 60 fps on integrated GPU, dpr capped
172:   at 1.5, no shadow maps, Html labels capped near 20 with distance
173:   culling.
174: - Everything bundled for offline booths; no runtime network calls
175:   required (network allowed as a bonus, never a dependency).

1: # profiles.json Schema (Phase E1 Artifact)
2: 
3: Field by field contract for the Phase E2 loader. The artifact lives at
4: `public/data/engine/profiles.json`, is written by
5: `uv run python -m scripts.engine.build`, and is gated by
6: `uv run python -m scripts.engine.verify`.
7: 
8: ## Guarantees
9: 
10: - Compact JSON (no spaces), one trailing newline, LF line endings.
11: - No timestamps and no floating point values anywhere: two consecutive
12:   builds of unchanged sources are byte identical.
13: - `profiles` keys are account id strings in ascending numeric order.
14: - Every money value is an integer in CAD cents. Every runway value is an
15:   integer count of tenths of a month.
16: - Sources are verified against `data/tangerine/SHA256SUMS` before any row
17:   is read; a mismatch fails the build loudly.
18: 
19: ## Top level shape
20: 
21: ```json
22: {
23:   "meta": {
24:     "schema_version": 1,
25:     "generated_by": "scripts.engine.build",
26:     "sources": [
27:       {"path": "data/tangerine/monthly_summary.csv", "sha256": "64 hex chars", "rows": 185326},
28:       {"path": "data/tangerine/loans.csv", "sha256": "64 hex chars", "rows": 682},
29:       {"path": "data/tangerine/accounts.csv", "sha256": "64 hex chars", "rows": 4500}
30:     ],
31:     "account_count": 4500,
32:     "date_range": {"start": "2020-01", "end": "2025-12"},
33:     "money_unit": "integer CAD cents",
34:     "runway_unit": "tenths of a month",
35:     "rounding": "...",
36:     "definitions": {"income_cents": "...", "runway_deci_months": "..."},
37:     "checksum_recipe": "...",
38:     "edge_flag_counts": {"pensioner": 740, "thin_history": 377, "zero_income": 14,
39:                          "defaulted_loan": 45, "negative_buffer": 23}
40:   },
41:   "profiles": {
42:     "20111": {"account_id": "20111", "income_cents": 0}
43:   }
44: }
45: ```
46: 
47: ## meta block
48: 
49: - `schema_version` (int): currently `1`. The E2 loader must refuse any
50:   other value instead of guessing.
51: - `generated_by` (string): always `scripts.engine.build`.
52: - `sources` (array of 3): one entry per canonical CSV in fixed order
53:   (monthly_summary, loans, accounts) with `path`, `sha256` (64 lowercase
54:   hex), `rows` (data rows, header excluded).
55: - `account_count` (int): equals the number of entries in `profiles`.
56: - `date_range` (object): `start` and `end` as `YYYY-MM`, the minimum
57:   `history.first_month` and maximum `history.last_month` over all
58:   profiles.
59: - `money_unit` (string): `integer CAD cents`.
60: - `runway_unit` (string): `tenths of a month`, so 1200 means 120.0
61:   months.
62: - `rounding` (string): the human readable rounding contract. Dollars
63:   convert to cents with `np.rint(dollars * 100)` (half to even), and
64:   every median, mean, and runway division afterwards uses
65:   ROUND_HALF_UP (ties away from zero) exactly once at the metric
66:   boundary.
67: - `definitions` (object): judge definitions for `income_cents`,
68:   `fixed_costs_cents`, `spending_cents`, `buffer_cents`,
69:   `household_bills_cents`, `loan_payment_cents`, `gap_cents`,
70:   `runway_deci_months`. These strings are duplicated on purpose in
71:   `scripts/engine/verify.py`; drift fails verification.
72: - `checksum_recipe` (string): the provenance recipe (see below).
73: - `edge_flag_counts` (object): accounts per flag across the whole
74:   dataset. The E2 UI should treat a count of 0 as "this flag never fires
75:   in this data". All five are nonzero in the shipped build.
76: 
77: ## profiles entry (one per account)
78: 
79: Exactly these keys, no more, no less:
80: 
81: ### Identity and judge metrics
82: 
83: - `account_id` (string): digits, matches the key.
84: - `income_cents` (int): I, median of `money_in` over all monthly rows.
85: - `fixed_costs_cents` (int): F, median over months of the per row sum
86:   `household_bills + insurance + loan_payments`. Part 1 display only,
87:   never used in the runway.
88: - `spending_cents` (int): S, median of `money_out` over all rows.
89: - `buffer_cents` (int): B, mean of `avg_daily_balance` over the last
90:   `min(6, n)` rows sorted by month, rounded half up. May be negative.
91: - `household_bills_cents` (int): H, median of `household_bills`.
92: - `loan_payment_cents` (int): P, `monthly_payment` when the loan status
93:   is `C` or `D` (running at the end of 2025), otherwise 0. Accounts with
94:   no loan are 0.
95: - `insurance_cents` (int): median of `insurance`.
96: - `loan_payments_median_cents` (int): median of `loan_payments`.
97: - `pension_in_cents` (int): sum of `pension_in` over all rows, not a
98:   median and not windowed.
99: - `gap_cents` (int): S minus I. Positive means typical spending exceeds
100:   typical income.
101: 
102: ### Runway (baseline, before any shock)
103: 
104: - `runway_state` (string): exactly one of `finite`, `no_shortfall`,
105:   `buffer_depleted`.
106: - `runway_deci_months` (int): 0 for `buffer_depleted`, 1200 for
107:   `no_shortfall`, otherwise `ROUND_HALF_UP(10 * buffer_left / gap)`
108:   capped at 1200. Branch order is fixed: `buffer_left <= 0` first, then
109:   `gap <= 0`, then the finite branch. The E3 shock engine must reuse
110:   this branch order so live shock numbers match the artifact baseline.
111: 
112: ### history
113: 
114: - `history.first_month`, `history.last_month` (string): `YYYY-MM`.
115: - `history.row_count` (int): monthly rows, at least 1, at most 72.
116: - `history.months_contiguous` (bool): true when the sorted months fill
117:   one unbroken span (true for every account in the shipped build).
118: - `history.months` (array of `YYYY-MM`, optional): present only when
119:   `months_contiguous` is false, one entry per row in month order.
120: 
121: ### loan
122: 
123: `null` when the account has no row in `loans.csv`, otherwise an object:
124: 
125: - `loan_id` (int), `status` (string `A`, `B`, `C`, `D`),
126:   `defaulted` (bool, true for `B` and `D`),
127:   `amount_cents` (int), `duration_months` (int),
128:   `monthly_payment_cents` (int), `loan_start` (string `YYYY-MM-DD`),
129:   `scheduled_end_month` (string `YYYY-MM`, `loan_start` month plus
130:   `duration_months`).
131: 
132: The P rule reads `status` only: `C` or `D` pays, `A` or `B` is 0. The
133: build report logs the schedule versus status disagreement count so a
134: future data refresh that breaks the rule shows up immediately (0
135: disagreements in the shipped build).
136: 
137: ### flags
138: 
139: Exactly five booleans:
140: 
141: - `pensioner`: `pension_in_cents > 0`.
142: - `thin_history`: `row_count < 18`, a quarter of the 72 month dataset
143:   span. The B window itself is still `min(6, n)` rows regardless of this
144:   flag.
145: - `zero_income`: `income_cents == 0`.
146: - `defaulted_loan`: `loan.status == "D"` (no loan means false).
147: - `negative_buffer`: `buffer_cents < 0`.
148: 
149: ### balance_series
150: 
151: - `start_month` (string): month of the first value.
152: - `values_cents` (array of int): the last `min(12, row_count)`
153:   `avg_daily_balance` values in month order. Chart input for the E2
154:   profile view.
155: 
156: ### provenance
157: 
158: - `source` (string): `data/tangerine/monthly_summary.csv`.
159: - `filter` (string): `account_id = <id> ordered by month ascending`.
160: - `agg` (string): judge aggregation text, ends with
161:   `checksum value = money_in_cents`.
162: - `check_sum` (string): 64 lowercase hex.
163: 
164: Recompute recipe (mirrored by `src/data/checksum.ts`): build row ids
165: `<account_id>:<month>`, sort them ascending, pair each with the row's
166: `money_in` in cents, join `id:value` lines with a single LF, SHA256 the
167: UTF-8 bytes.
168: 
169: ## E2 loader validation checklist
170: 
171: 1. `JSON.parse` the fetch of `profiles.json` (single bundled file, no
172:    runtime network beyond the static asset).
173: 2. Refuse unless `schema_version === 1` and the top level keys are
174:    exactly `meta` and `profiles`.
175: 3. For each entry, check the key set above, integer money fields (not
176:    `NaN`, not fractional), `runway_state` enum, `runway_deci_months` in
177:    `[0, 1200]`, five boolean flags, `provenance.check_sum` hex length 64.
178: 4. Check `meta.account_count === Object.keys(profiles).length`.
179: 5. Keys arrive in numeric order already; a search index may assume it.
180: 
181: ## Regeneration and verification
182: 
183: ```bash
184: uv run python -m scripts.engine.build     # writes the artifact and prints the report
185: uv run python -m scripts.engine.verify    # naive csv recompute, drift diff, dash scan, SHA256
186: uv run pytest scripts/engine -q           # golden fixtures, schema, determinism
187: ```

1: # [Tangerine] Resilience Rewired
2: 
3: Tangerine Track · Sheridan Datathon 2026 · November 7-8
4: 
5: Build a financial resilience engine for real bank customers.
6: 
7: This track is powered by Tangerine. At judging, a judge will pick a customer and a scenario, and you will run your engine live.
8: 
9: ---
10: 
11: ## The data
12: 
13: `data/` holds real, anonymized data from a bank: 4,500 accounts, about 1.06 million transactions and 682 loans and how each one is going.
14: 
15: ---
16: 
17: ## The challenge
18: 
19: Build a tool that does three things. It can be a dashboard, an app, a notebook, an AI agent or anything else.
20: 
21: 1. **Know the customer.** Take any `account_id` and show their income, bills and fixed costs, savings buffer, and months of runway.
22: 2. **Take a shock.** Apply a shock and recalculate, for example a job loss with EI, higher rent or household bills, a surprise repair, or a mix. Let the user change the size of the shock.
23: 3. **Make a plan.** Give that customer a goal plan, like building an emergency fund, and a backup plan for if the shock hits, both based on their own numbers.
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## How judging works
28: 
29: **Discovery 35%, Data Use 25%, Communication 25%, Impact 15%**.
30: 
31: You get about 5 minutes:
32: 
33: | Time | What happens |
34: | :-- | :-- |
35: | 1 min | **Pitch:** show your engine and your biggest finding |
36: | 3 min | **Live twist:** a judge picks an `account_id` and reads a twist card. You run it live and explain the new numbers and plan |
37: | 1 min | **Questions** from the judges |
38: 
39:  
40: 
41: Example twists:
42: - "This customer was laid off. EI pays 55% of their usual income for 6 months. Do they make it?"
43: - "The furnace dies, and the repair costs a full month of their typical spending."
44: - "They lose their job (EI at 55%) and their household bills go up 15% in the same month."
45: 
46: ---
47: 
48: ## How judges calculate the numbers
49: 
50: Judges have answers worked out with these definitions, from `monthly_summary.csv`:
51: 
52: | Number | Definition |
53: | :-- | :-- |
54: | **Typical monthly money in** (I) | Median of `money_in` |
55: | **Typical fixed costs** (F) | Median of `household_bills + insurance + loan_payments` (shown in part 1, not used in runway) |
56: | **Typical monthly spending** (S) | Median of `money_out` |
57: | **Buffer** (B) | Mean of `avg_daily_balance` over the account's last 6 rows, sorted by month |
58: | **Household bills** (H) | Median of `household_bills` (rent and utility shocks change this) |
59: | **Loan payment** (P) | `monthly_payment` in `loans.csv` if the loan is still running at the end of 2025, otherwise 0 |
60: 
61: **Runway** (months) = buffer left after one-off costs ÷ monthly shortfall:
62: 
63: ```
64: buffer_left = B - one_off_costs
65: gap         = spending_after_shock - income_after_shock
66: if buffer_left <= 0:  runway = 0
67: elif gap <= 0:        runway = "no shortfall (120+)"
68: else:                 runway = min(buffer_left / gap, 120)
69: ```
70: 
71: Runway is rounded to 1 decimal. A shock changes income or spending in this formula: for example, a job loss with EI at 55% means income = 0.55 × I, and household bills up 15% means spending = S + 0.15 × H.
72: 
73: You can use your own definitions instead. If your numbers differ from these, be ready to explain why.
74: 
75: ---
76: 
77: ## Using AI
78: 
79: Use any tools you want, including AI.
80: 
81: ---
82: 
83: ## What to submit (on Devpost)
84: 
85: 1. **Demo video** (2 to 3 minutes) of your engine running.
86: 2. **Code repo** (public link or zip).
87: 3. **Short write-up:** what your engine does and your biggest finding.
88: 4. **Sources:** links to every outside data source you used.
89: 
90: ---
91: 
92: ## Data dictionary
93: 
94: All files are in `data/` and link through the ID columns. **All money columns are in Canadian dollars.**
95: 
96: ```
97: districts ──< accounts ──< transactions
98:                 │    ├──< monthly_summary
99:                 │    ├──< standing_orders
100:                 │    └──< loans
101:                 └──< dispositions >── clients
102:                           └──< cards
103: ```
104: 
105: ### `monthly_summary.csv` (185,326 rows)
106: One row per account per month, built from `transactions.csv`, from the account's first transaction month to its last (quiet months included). Balances are end-of-day balances, carried forward on days with no activity.
107: 
108: | Column | Meaning |
109: | :-- | :-- |
110: | `account_id`, `month` | Account and month (`YYYY-MM`) |
111: | `money_in`, `money_out` | Total money in and total money out (positive numbers) |
112: | `cash_deposits`, `transfers_in`, `pension_in`, `interest_in` | Parts of `money_in` (`transfers_in` excludes pensions); they add up to `money_in` |
113: | `household_bills`, `insurance`, `loan_payments`, `bank_fees`, `cash_withdrawals_genuine`, `card_withdrawals`, `transfers_out_other` | Parts of `money_out` (`transfers_out_other` = unlabelled transfers out); they add up to `money_out` |
114: | `month_end_balance` | End-of-day balance on the last day of the month |
115: | `min_balance`, `avg_daily_balance` | Lowest and average end-of-day balance in the month (the first month counts from the first transaction) |
116: | `days_below_zero` | Days in the month that ended with a negative balance |
117: 
118: ### `transactions.csv` (1,056,320 rows, about 100 MB)
119: | Column | Meaning |
120: | :-- | :-- |
121: | `transaction_id`, `account_id` | Transaction and its account |
122: | `date` | Date (2020-01-01 to 2025-12-31) |
123: | `direction` | `credit (money in)` or `debit (money out)` |
124: | `operation` | `cash deposit`, `cash withdrawal`, `card withdrawal`, `transfer in from another bank`, `transfer out to another bank`, `bill payment`, `bank fee`, `interest` |
125: | `purpose` | When known: `household bills`, `insurance`, `loan payment`, `pension`, `interest credited`, `statement fee`, `penalty interest (negative balance)`. Blank = not labelled |
126: | `amount` | Amount, always positive |
127: | `signed_amount` | Positive = money in, negative = money out |
128: | `balance` | Account balance after the transaction. Rows within the same day are not in time order |
129: | `partner_bank`, `partner_account` | For transfers: the other bank (two-letter code) and the account number at that bank (not an `account_id` here). Blank or 0 when not a transfer. Read `partner_bank` as text |
130: 
131: `bank fee` = statement fees and penalty interest. `bill payment` = household bills or insurance paid at the bank.
132: 
133: ### `loans.csv` (682 rows)
134: | Column | Meaning |
135: | :-- | :-- |
136: | `loan_id`, `account_id` | Loan and the account that took it (one loan per account) |
137: | `loan_start` | Date the loan was granted |
138: | `amount`, `duration_months`, `monthly_payment` | Size, length in months, and monthly payment (`amount` = `duration_months` × `monthly_payment`) |
139: | `status`, `status_meaning` | A = finished, repaid; B = finished, NOT repaid (default); C = running, OK so far; D = running, client in debt |
140: | `defaulted` | 1 if B or D, 0 if A or C |
141: 
142: ### Other files
143: | File | Rows | Columns and notes |
144: | :-- | --: | :-- |
145: | `accounts.csv` | 4,500 | `account_id`, `district_id` (branch), `frequency` (statement frequency), `account_opened` |
146: | `clients.csv` | 5,369 | `client_id`, `gender`, `birth_date`, `district_id` (home) |
147: | `dispositions.csv` | 5,369 | `disposition_id`, `client_id`, `account_id`, `type` (`owner` or `authorized user`) |

1: # [Tangerine] Resilience Rewired
2: 
3: Tangerine Track · Sheridan Datathon 2026 · November 7-8
4: 
5: Build a financial resilience engine for real bank customers.
6: 
7: This track is powered by Tangerine. At judging, a judge will pick a customer and a scenario, and you will run your engine live.
8: 
9: ---
10: 
11: ## The data
12: 
13: `data/` holds real, anonymized data from a bank: 4,500 accounts, about 1.06 million transactions and 682 loans and how each one is going.
14: 
15: ---
16: 
17: ## The challenge
18: 
19: Build a tool that does three things. It can be a dashboard, an app, a notebook, an AI agent or anything else.
20: 
21: 1. **Know the customer.** Take any `account_id` and show their income, bills and fixed costs, savings buffer, and months of runway.
22: 2. **Take a shock.** Apply a shock and recalculate, for example a job loss with EI, higher rent or household bills, a surprise repair, or a mix. Let the user change the size of the shock.
23: 3. **Make a plan.** Give that customer a goal plan, like building an emergency fund, and a backup plan for if the shock hits, both based on their own numbers.
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## How judging works
28: 
29: **Discovery 35%, Data Use 25%, Communication 25%, Impact 15%**.
30: 
31: You get about 5 minutes:
32: 
33: | Time | What happens |
34: | :-- | :-- |
35: | 1 min | **Pitch:** show your engine and your biggest finding |
36: | 3 min | **Live twist:** a judge picks an `account_id` and reads a twist card. You run it live and explain the new numbers and plan |
37: | 1 min | **Questions** from the judges |
38: 
39:  
40: 
41: Example twists:
42: - "This customer was laid off. EI pays 55% of their usual income for 6 months. Do they make it?"
43: - "The furnace dies, and the repair costs a full month of their typical spending."
44: - "They lose their job (EI at 55%) and their household bills go up 15% in the same month."
45: 
46: ---
47: 
48: ## How judges calculate the numbers
49: 
50: Judges have answers worked out with these definitions, from `monthly_summary.csv`:
51: 
52: | Number | Definition |
53: | :-- | :-- |
54: | **Typical monthly money in** (I) | Median of `money_in` |
55: | **Typical fixed costs** (F) | Median of `household_bills + insurance + loan_payments` (shown in part 1, not used in runway) |
56: | **Typical monthly spending** (S) | Median of `money_out` |
57: | **Buffer** (B) | Mean of `avg_daily_balance` over the account's last 6 rows, sorted by month |
58: | **Household bills** (H) | Median of `household_bills` (rent and utility shocks change this) |
59: | **Loan payment** (P) | `monthly_payment` in `loans.csv` if the loan is still running at the end of 2025, otherwise 0 |
60: 
61: **Runway** (months) = buffer left after one-off costs ÷ monthly shortfall:
62: 
63: ```
64: buffer_left = B - one_off_costs
65: gap         = spending_after_shock - income_after_shock
66: if buffer_left <= 0:  runway = 0
67: elif gap <= 0:        runway = "no shortfall (120+)"
68: else:                 runway = min(buffer_left / gap, 120)
69: ```
70: 
71: Runway is rounded to 1 decimal. A shock changes income or spending in this formula: for example, a job loss with EI at 55% means income = 0.55 × I, and household bills up 15% means spending = S + 0.15 × H.
72: 
73: You can use your own definitions instead. If your numbers differ from these, be ready to explain why.
74: 
75: ---
76: 
77: ## Using AI
78: 
79: Use any tools you want, including AI.

199: ## Nov 07 2026 - Phase E1: Profile precompute contract for the resilience engine
200: 
201: **Context**: live judging needs every judge number for any account_id
202: computed before the booth opens, with the exact branch rules of
203: docs/tangerine-challenge.md, and the E1 build was resumed from an
204: interrupted session. Reviewing the on-disk modules against the checklist
205: surfaced two places where the checklist could not hold against the real
206: data: the thin_history flag was defined as fewer than 6 monthly rows
207: while the shortest real account history is 12 rows (so the flag would
208: never fire), and the requested fixture "pensioner with running loan
209: status C" cannot exist because all 740 accounts with pension_in above
210: zero have no row in loans.csv at all.
211: 
212: **Decision**: ship public/data/engine/profiles.json as the E1 contract:
213: compact deterministic JSON (no timestamps, no floats, accounts in
214: numeric key order) with a meta block (schema_version, sources with
215: sha256 and rows, account_count, date_range, units, rounding, judge
216: definitions, checksum recipe, edge flag counts) and one 18 key profile
217: per account carrying the judge metrics in integer cents, the baseline
218: runway, history, the loan record, the five flags, the last 12 balances,
219: and a provenance check_sum. P reads loans.csv status only (C or D pays,
220: otherwise 0) and the build report logs the status versus schedule
221: disagreement count (448 running by status, 448 by schedule, 0
222: disagreements). thin_history is redefined as row_count below 18, a
223: quarter of the 72 month dataset span, which fires on 377 accounts and
224: makes the flag meaningful for the E2 caveat UI; the B window stays
225: min(6, n) rows regardless. Five golden fixture accounts (68257, 23838,
226: 49900, 98952, 42988) are frozen in scripts/engine/golden_fixtures.json
227: with visible workings (sorted cents arrays, median steps, runway long
228: division), covering odd and even medians, the half cent tie, thin
229: history with zero income, a running loan C, a defaulted loan D, every
230: flag, and all three runway branches; the pensioner fixture has no loan
231: and the impossibility is recorded in the fixture notes. verify.py
232: recomputes all 4500 accounts with the naive csv module (no pandas, no
233: numpy, no import of metrics), diffs field by field, scans for dash
234: violations, and prints the artifact SHA256; tests pin the fixtures to
235: both metrics() and the shipped artifact, recompute check_sum for every
236: account, validate the schema, and prove two consecutive builds are byte
237: identical.
238: 
239: **Rationale**: judges calculate with these exact definitions, so a
240: precomputed artifact is only useful if its numbers are reproducible by
241: an independent implementation; the flag threshold change is the smallest
242: edit that makes a checklist requirement true on real data instead of
243: documenting a flag that never fires; frozen hand computed fixtures make
244: any future rule drift fail a test rather than pass review.
245: 
246: **Trade-offs**: the 4.7 MB artifact lives in the repo and must be
247: regenerated whenever a source checksum changes (fixtures freeze five
248: account ids, so a data refresh means re-deriving them); the thin_history
249: threshold is tied to this dataset's 72 month span and must be revisited
250: if the span changes; status C or D for P can diverge from the amortization
251: schedule on future data (the disagreement counter is the tripwire);
252: plans.py stays a dormant draft until E4, keeping E1 to the precompute
253: contract only.

469: function metricF1(section: Record<string, unknown>, key: string): ReportMetric {
470:   const numbers = numbersOf(section, key)
471:   const share = asNumber(numbers.structuralShareOfAnnualSpend, `${key}.numbers.structuralShareOfAnnualSpend`)
472:   const structural = stringList(numbers.structuralCategories, `${key}.numbers.structuralCategories`)
473:   const structuralSpend = asInteger(numbers.structuralSpendCents, `${key}.numbers.structuralSpendCents`)
474:   const totalSpend = asInteger(numbers.totalAnnualSpendCents, `${key}.numbers.totalAnnualSpendCents`)
475:   return {
476:     value: `${(share * 100).toFixed(2)}%`,
477:     label: 'of annual spend is structural',
478:     note: `${structural.join(' and ')} account for ${formatCents(structuralSpend)} of ${formatCents(totalSpend)}`,
479:   }
480: }

482: function metricF2(section: Record<string, unknown>, key: string): ReportMetric {
483:   const numbers = numbersOf(section, key)
484:   const category = asString(numbers.strongestCalendarCategory, `${key}.numbers.strongestCalendarCategory`)
485:   const lift = asNumber(numbers.strongestCalendarLift, `${key}.numbers.strongestCalendarLift`)
486:   const windowDays = asInteger(numbers.holidayWindowDays, `${key}.numbers.holidayWindowDays`)
487:   const categories = recordList(section.categories, `${key}.categories`)
488:   const match = categories.find((entry) => entry.name === category)
489:   const holidayShare = match
490:     ? asNumber(
491:         asRecord(match.holidayWindow, `${key}.categories[].holidayWindow`).share,
492:         `${key}.categories[].holidayWindow.share`,
493:       )
494:     : 0
495:   return {
496:     value: `${lift.toFixed(2)}x`,
497:     label: `holiday lift for ${category} (strongest calendar category)`,
498:     note: `${(holidayShare * 100).toFixed(1)}% of ${category} spend lands in the ${windowDays} day holiday window`,
499:   }
500: }

562: function parseF1(root: Record<string, unknown>): F1Section {
563:   const key = 'f1StructuralVsDiscretionary'
564:   const section = asRecord(root[key], `findings.${key}`)
565:   const numbers = numbersOf(section, key)
566:   const method = methodOf(section, key)
567:   const chartTwin = chartTwinOf(section, key)
568:   const lags = numberList(chartTwin.lags, `${key}.chartTwin.lags`)
569:   const lagWindow = asArray(chartTwin.lagWindow, `${key}.chartTwin.lagWindow`)
570:   if (lagWindow.length !== 2) {
571:     throw new Error(`${key}.chartTwin.lagWindow must have two entries`)
572:   }
573:   const categoryBars = recordList(section.categories, `${key}.categories`).map((entry, index) => {
574:     const name = asString(entry.name, `${key}.categories[${index}].name`)
575:     const classification = asClassification(
576:       entry.classification,
577:       `${key}.categories[${index}].classification`,
578:     )
579:     return {
580:       name,
581:       annualSpendCents: asInteger(entry.annualSpendCents, `${key}.categories[${index}].annualSpendCents`),
582:       debitRows: asInteger(entry.debitRows, `${key}.categories[${index}].debitRows`),
583:       classification,
584:       eligibleForLagTest: entry.eligibleForLagTest === true,
585:       peakAcf: asNumber(entry.peakAcf, `${key}.categories[${index}].peakAcf`),
586:       peakLag: asInteger(entry.peakLag, `${key}.categories[${index}].peakLag`),
587:       threshold: asNumber(entry.threshold, `${key}.categories[${index}].threshold`),
588:       reason: asString(entry.reason, `${key}.categories[${index}].reason`),
589:     }
590:   })
591:   const acfSeries = recordList(chartTwin.series, `${key}.chartTwin.series`).map((entry, index) => {
592:     const classification = asClassification(
593:       entry.classification,
594:       `${key}.chartTwin.series[${index}].classification`,
595:     )
596:     const acf = numberList(entry.acf, `${key}.chartTwin.series[${index}].acf`)
597:     if (acf.length !== lags.length) {
598:       throw new Error(`${key}.chartTwin.series[${index}].acf must match chartTwin.lags in length`)
599:     }
600:     return {
601:       name: asString(entry.name, `${key}.chartTwin.series[${index}].name`),
602:       classification,
603:       acf,
604:       threshold: asNumber(entry.threshold, `${key}.chartTwin.series[${index}].threshold`),
605:     }
606:   })
607:   return {
608:     id: 'F1',
609:     key,
610:     question: questionOf(section, key),
611:     method,
612:     methodOneLiner: firstSentence(method),
613:     limitations: limitationsOf(section, key),
614:     headline: headlineFor('F1', root),
615:     metric: metricF1(section, key),
616:     structuralShareOfAnnualSpend: asNumber(
617:       numbers.structuralShareOfAnnualSpend,
618:       `${key}.numbers.structuralShareOfAnnualSpend`,
619:     ),
620:     discretionaryShareOfAnnualSpend: asNumber(
621:       numbers.discretionaryShareOfAnnualSpend,
622:       `${key}.numbers.discretionaryShareOfAnnualSpend`,
623:     ),
624:     totalAnnualSpendCents: asInteger(numbers.totalAnnualSpendCents, `${key}.numbers.totalAnnualSpendCents`),
625:     structuralSpendCents: asInteger(numbers.structuralSpendCents, `${key}.numbers.structuralSpendCents`),
626:     discretionarySpendCents: asInteger(
627:       numbers.discretionarySpendCents,
628:       `${key}.numbers.discretionarySpendCents`,
629:     ),
630:     structuralCategories: stringList(numbers.structuralCategories, `${key}.numbers.structuralCategories`),
631:     discretionaryCategories: stringList(
632:       numbers.discretionaryCategories,
633:       `${key}.numbers.discretionaryCategories`,
634:     ),
635:     lagWindowDays: [
636:       asInteger(lagWindow[0], `${key}.chartTwin.lagWindow[0]`),
637:       asInteger(lagWindow[1], `${key}.chartTwin.lagWindow[1]`),
638:     ],
639:     minimumDebitRows: asInteger(numbers.minimumDebitRows, `${key}.numbers.minimumDebitRows`),
640:     lags,
641:     categoryBars,
642:     acfSeries,
643:   }
644: }

646: function parseF2(root: Record<string, unknown>): F2Section {
647:   const key = 'f2Seasonality'
648:   const section = asRecord(root[key], `findings.${key}`)
649:   const numbers = numbersOf(section, key)
650:   const chartTwin = chartTwinOf(section, key)
651:   const strongest = asString(numbers.strongestCalendarCategory, `${key}.numbers.strongestCalendarCategory`)
652:   const monthLabels = stringList(chartTwin.monthLabels, `${key}.chartTwin.monthLabels`)
653:   const monthShares = recordList(chartTwin.monthShares, `${key}.chartTwin.monthShares`).map(
654:     (entry, index) => ({
655:       name: asString(entry.name, `${key}.chartTwin.monthShares[${index}].name`),
656:       shares: numberList(entry.shares, `${key}.chartTwin.monthShares[${index}].shares`),
657:     }),
658:   )
659:   const strongestSeries = monthShares.find((entry) => entry.name === strongest)
660:   if (!strongestSeries) {
661:     throw new Error(`${key}.chartTwin.monthShares must carry the strongest calendar category`)
662:   }
663:   if (strongestSeries.shares.length !== monthLabels.length) {
664:     throw new Error(`${key}.chartTwin.monthShares must match chartTwin.monthLabels in length`)
665:   }
666:   const categories = recordList(section.categories, `${key}.categories`)
667:   const strongestCategory = categories.find((entry) => entry.name === strongest)
668:   if (!strongestCategory) {
669:     throw new Error(`${key}.categories must carry the strongest calendar category`)
670:   }
671:   const calendarMonthShares = numberList(
672:     strongestCategory.monthDayShares,
673:     `${key}.categories[].monthDayShares`,
674:   )
675:   if (calendarMonthShares.length !== monthLabels.length) {
676:     throw new Error(`${key}.categories[].monthDayShares must match chartTwin.monthLabels in length`)
677:   }
678:   const holidayWindow = asRecord(strongestCategory.holidayWindow, `${key}.categories[].holidayWindow`)
679:   return {
680:     id: 'F2',
681:     key,
682:     question: questionOf(section, key),
683:     method: methodOf(section, key),
684:     methodOneLiner: firstSentence(methodOf(section, key)),
685:     limitations: limitationsOf(section, key),
686:     headline: headlineFor('F2', root),
687:     metric: metricF2(section, key),
688:     overallVerdict: asString(numbers.overallVerdict, `${key}.numbers.overallVerdict`),
689:     verdictSummary: asString(numbers.verdictSummary, `${key}.numbers.verdictSummary`),
690:     strongestCalendarCategory: strongest,
691:     strongestCalendarLift: asNumber(numbers.strongestCalendarLift, `${key}.numbers.strongestCalendarLift`),
692:     strongestBehavioralCategory: asString(
693:       numbers.strongestBehavioralCategory,
694:       `${key}.numbers.strongestBehavioralCategory`,
695:     ),
696:     strongestBehavioralDeviation: asNumber(
697:       numbers.strongestBehavioralDeviation,
698:       `${key}.numbers.strongestBehavioralDeviation`,
699:     ),
700:     holidayWindowDays: asInteger(numbers.holidayWindowDays, `${key}.numbers.holidayWindowDays`),
701:     holidayWindowStart: asString(holidayWindow.start, `${key}.categories[].holidayWindow.start`),
702:     holidayWindowEnd: asString(holidayWindow.end, `${key}.categories[].holidayWindow.end`),
703:     holidayLiftThreshold: asNumber(numbers.holidayLiftThreshold, `${key}.numbers.holidayLiftThreshold`),
704:     weeklyDeviationThreshold: asNumber(
705:       numbers.weeklyDeviationThreshold,
706:       `${key}.numbers.weeklyDeviationThreshold`,
707:     ),
708:     minimumWeeklyRows: asInteger(numbers.minimumWeeklyRows, `${key}.numbers.minimumWeeklyRows`),
709:     monthLabels,
710:     monthShares,
711:     calendarMonthShares,
712:     strongestHolidayShare: asNumber(holidayWindow.share, `${key}.categories[].holidayWindow.share`),
713:     categoryVerdicts: categories.map((entry, index) => ({
714:       name: asString(entry.name, `${key}.categories[${index}].name`),
715:       verdict: asString(entry.verdict, `${key}.categories[${index}].verdict`),
716:     })),
717:   }
718: }

720: function parseF3(root: Record<string, unknown>): F3Section {
721:   const key = 'f3DeficitRisk'
722:   const section = asRecord(root[key], `findings.${key}`)
723:   const numbers = numbersOf(section, key)
724:   const chartTwin = chartTwinOf(section, key)
725:   const roc = asRecord(chartTwin.roc, `${key}.chartTwin.roc`)
726:   const confusion = asRecord(numbers.confusion, `${key}.numbers.confusion`)
727:   const chartCoefficients = recordList(chartTwin.coefficients, `${key}.chartTwin.coefficients`)
728:   const coefficients = recordList(section.coefficients, `${key}.coefficients`).map(
729:     (entry, index) => ({
730:       feature: asString(entry.feature, `${key}.coefficients[${index}].feature`),
731:       coefficient: asNumber(
732:         entry.standardizedCoefficient,

735:       direction: asString(entry.direction, `${key}.coefficients[${index}].direction`),

737:   )

739:   const chartCoefficientFeatures = chartCoefficients.map((entry, index) => {
740:     const feature = asString(entry.feature, `${key}.chartTwin.coefficients[${index}].feature`)
741:     if (!byFeature.has(feature)) {

567:   const chartTwin = chartTwinOf(section, key)
568:   const lags = numberList(chartTwin.lags, `${key}.chartTwin.lags`)
569:   const lagWindow = asArray(chartTwin.lagWindow, `${key}.chartTwin.lagWindow`)
570:   if (lagWindow.length !== 2) {
571:     throw new Error(`${key}.chartTwin.lagWindow must have two entries`)
572:   }
573:   const categoryBars = recordList(section.categories, `${key}.categories`).map((entry, index) => {
574:     const name = asString(entry.name, `${key}.categories[${index}].name`)
575:     const classification = asClassification(
576:       entry.classification,
577:       `${key}.categories[${index}].classification`,
578:     )
579:     return {
580:       name,
581:       annualSpendCents: asInteger(entry.annualSpendCents, `${key}.categories[${index}].annualSpendCents`),
582:       debitRows: asInteger(entry.debitRows, `${key}.categories[${index}].debitRows`),
583:       classification,
584:       eligibleForLagTest: entry.eligibleForLagTest === true,
585:       peakAcf: asNumber(entry.peakAcf, `${key}.categories[${index}].peakAcf`),
586:       peakLag: asInteger(entry.peakLag, `${key}.categories[${index}].peakLag`),
587:       threshold: asNumber(entry.threshold, `${key}.categories[${index}].threshold`),
588:       reason: asString(entry.reason, `${key}.categories[${index}].reason`),
589:     }
590:   })
591:   const acfSeries = recordList(chartTwin.series, `${key}.chartTwin.series`).map((entry, index) => {
592:     const classification = asClassification(
593:       entry.classification,
594:       `${key}.chartTwin.series[${index}].classification`,
595:     )
596:     const acf = numberList(entry.acf, `${key}.chartTwin.series[${index}].acf`)
597:     if (acf.length !== lags.length) {
598:       throw new Error(`${key}.chartTwin.series[${index}].acf must match chartTwin.lags in length`)
599:     }
600:     return {
601:       name: asString(entry.name, `${key}.chartTwin.series[${index}].name`),
602:       classification,
603:       acf,
604:       threshold: asNumber(entry.threshold, `${key}.chartTwin.series[${index}].threshold`),
605:     }
606:   })
607:   return {
608:     id: 'F1',
609:     key,
610:     question: questionOf(section, key),
611:     method,
612:     methodOneLiner: firstSentence(method),
613:     limitations: limitationsOf(section, key),
614:     headline: headlineFor('F1', root),
615:     metric: metricF1(section, key),
616:     structuralShareOfAnnualSpend: asNumber(
617:       numbers.structuralShareOfAnnualSpend,

619:     ),

621:       numbers.discretionaryShareOfAnnualSpend,

623:     ),

625:     structuralSpendCents: asInteger(numbers.structuralSpendCents, `${key}.numbers.structuralSpendCents`),
